new_statements.quote: Stress must be considered to be extra emphasis or loudness and not length. For the most part, stress occurs on the last syllable of the word including those ending with a glottal stop as in (36). If, however, the word ends in a vowel, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable in (37) [p. 84]. ... In §6 we will see that stress occurs on the last syllable of the word if that syllable ends with a consonant. Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable when the word ends in a vowel. [pp. 80-81]
new_statements.citation: Pike, Eunice V. & Bernard Diatta. 1994. The phonology of Jóola Húluf. Journal of West African Languages 24(2): 77-84.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6 'Stress', p. 84 (PDF p. 8); also sec. 2.3 'Vowel sequences', pp. 80-81 (PDF pp. 4-5)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant (including glottal stop), and on the penultimate syllable when the word ends in a vowel; i.e. final closed syllables attract stress, otherwise penult. Examples p. 84: hobe'kel, ka'tah, e'sih, habe'be? vs. ka'sala, e'fengu, ege'lete, e'leli.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'for the most part'; sec. 2.3 notes that a sequence of like vowels (e.g. kale'en) behaves differently from a long vowel (ho'leen) for stress placement. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated words (citation forms); stress explicitly defined as loudness, distinct from length; pitch is separately described as predictable word/phrase contours (downglide, downstep, upstep) plus question-vs-statement intonation, so the language is treated as non-tonal. The lect is Jóola Húluf (Oussouye dept.), a dialect of Jola-Kasa, not Esulalu proper.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Jóola Húluf (Oussouye department, ~10,000 speakers, subgroups Ayuun/Húluf/Seelek), which Glottolog lists as the dialect hulu1244 under jola1262 (Jola-Esulalu = ISO csk Jola-Kasa). It is not the Esulalu dialect proper (esul1240); the Esulalu phonology (Sambou 1979) could not be opened. Glottolog itself files Pike & Diatta 1994 under jola1262.

sources.note: Sec. 6 'Stress' (p. 84): stress = loudness not length; for the most part on the last syllable of the word (incl. words ending in glottal stop); if the word ends in a vowel, stress is on the penultimate syllable. Sec. 2.3 (pp. 80-81) states the same rule (final syllable if consonant-final, penult if vowel-final) and notes that a sequence of like vowels behaves differently from a long vowel for stress. Sec. 5: predictable pitch contours (downglide/downstep/upstep) and question-vs-statement intonation; no lexical tone.

Bibliography only; confirms Sambou 1976 (CLAD 68, listed as 'Phonologie du nom diola-kasa essulaalu'), Sambou 1979 thesis, Sambou 2008 Sudlangues 10: 62-70, Pike & Diatta 1994, Wintz 1909, Diatta 1998.
Only lexicon features 129A/130A coded (source Wintz 1909); no stress features.
